questions.prompt: The 60-group rule scored a Sharpe ratio of 2.93 in-sample and 0.19 out-of-sample. What explains the fall?
options: The rule chose each group's side from about 17 days of noise, and that noise did not repeat
The out-of-sample period was too short to compute a Sharpe ratio
questions.explanation: The returns were random, so each group's in-sample average was noise. The rule fitted that noise perfectly in-sample, and new data brought new noise.

questions.prompt: Your rule scores well with a 50-day moving average, but badly with 45 or 55 days. What does that suggest?
options: The 50-day setting has found a real and precise edge
The rule is probably fitted to noise, because a real pattern would not depend on one exact setting
questions.explanation: A pattern that repeats should still show with nearby settings. A result that only one exact value produces is a sign the rule fits the wiggles of this history.

questions.prompt: Across 500 made-up histories, which rule had the bigger gap between its in-sample and out-of-sample Sharpe ratio?
options: Both had the same gap, because neither had an edge
questions.explanation: Both rules had no edge, so both scored about 0 out-of-sample. The rule with 60 parameters fitted far more noise, so its in-sample score was 3.07 higher than its out-of-sample score.
